entries.66190731ccdbee533b6f70f35c2130634e4e6deb: <div sID="gen6734" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="1Kgs.11" sID="1Kgs.11"/> <div eID="gen6734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6735" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6736" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with as melancholy a "but" as almost any we find in all the Bible. Hitherto we have read nothing of Solomon but what was great and good; but the lustre both of his goodness and of his greatness is here sullied and eclipsed, and his sun sets under a cloud. I. The glory of his piety is stained by his departure from God and his duty, in his latter days, marrying strange wives and worshipping strange gods, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.4-1Kgs.11.8">ver. 4-8</reference>. II. The glory of his prosperity is stained by God's displeasure against him and the fruits of that displeasure. 1. He sent him an angry message, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.9-1Kgs.11.13">ver. 9-13</reference>. 2. He stirred up enemies, who gave him disturbance, Hadad (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.14-1Kgs.11.22">ver. 14-22</reference>), Rezon, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.23-1Kgs.11.25">ver. 23-25</reference>. 3. He gave away ten tribes of his twelve, from his posterity after him, to Jeroboam, whom therefore he sought in vain to slay (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.26-1Kgs.11.40">ver. 26-40</reference>), and this is all that remains here to be told concerning Solomon, except his death and burial (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.41-1Kgs.11.43">ver. 41-43</reference>), for there is nothing perfect under the sun, but all is so above the sun.
entries.92764ce19af044be8f8a54c8cd02c3fdce845d7a: <div eID="gen6736" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6735" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Solomon's Defection and Degeneracy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 983.)</title> <div sID="gen6737" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> But king Solomon loved many strange women, together with the daughter of Pharaoh, women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Zidonians, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Hittites; <hi type="super">2</hi> Of the nations <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto the children of Israel, Ye shall not go in to them, neither shall they come in unto you: <hi type="italic">for</hi> surely they will turn away your heart after their gods: Solomon clave unto these in love. <hi type="super">3</hi> And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart. <hi type="super">4</hi> For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, <hi type="italic">that</hi> his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God, as <hi type="italic">was</hi> the heart of David his father. <hi type="super">5</hi> For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Solomon did evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and went not fully after the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , as <hi type="italic">did</hi> David his father. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then did Solomon build a high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, in the hill that <hi type="italic">is</hi> before Jerusalem, and for Molech, the abomination of the children of Ammon. <hi type="super">8</hi> And likewise did he for all his strange wives, which burnt incense and sacrificed unto their gods. <div eID="gen6737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6738" type="x-p"/> This is a sad story, and very surprising, of Solomon's defection and degeneracy. <div eID="gen6738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6739" type="x-p"/> I. Let us enquire into the occasions and particulars of it. Shall Solomon fall, that was the beauty of Israel, and so great a blessing of his generation? Yes, it is too true, and the scripture is faithful in relating it, and repeating it, and referring to it long after, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.26">Neh. xiii. 26</reference>. <hi type="italic">There was no king like Solomon who was beloved of his God, yet even him did outlandish women cause to sin.</hi> There is the summary of his apostasy; it was the woman that <hi type="italic">deceived him,</hi> and was <hi type="italic">first in the transgression.</hi> <div eID="gen6739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6740" type="x-p"/> 1. He doted on strange women, <hi type="italic">many strange women.</hi> Here his revolt began. (1.) He gave himself to women, which his mother had particularly cautioned him against. <reference osisRef="Prov.31.3">Prov. xxxi. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">Give not thy strength unto women</hi> (perhaps alluding to Samson, who lost his strength by giving information of it to a woman), for it is that which, as much as any thing, destroys kings. His father David's fall began with the lusts of the flesh, which he should have taken warning by. The love of women has <hi type="italic">cast down many wounded</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.26">Prov. vii. 26</reference>) and <hi type="italic">many</hi> (says bishop Hall) <hi type="italic">have had their head broken by their own rib.</hi> (2.) He took many women, so many that, at last, they amounted to 700 wives and 300 concubines, 1000 in all, and not one good one among them, as he himself owns in his penitential sermon (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.28">Eccl. vii. 28</reference>), for no woman of established virtue would be one of such a set. God had, by his law, particularly forbidden the kings to multiply either horses or wives, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.16-Deut.17.17">Deut. xvii. 16, 17</reference>. How he broke the former law, in multiplying horses, and having them <hi type="italic">out of Egypt</hi> too (which was expressly prohibited in that law) we read <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.29">ch. x. 29</reference>, and here we are told how he broke the latter (which proved of more fatal consequence) in multiplying wives. Note, Less sins, made gold with, open the door to greater. David had multiplied wives too much, and perhaps that made Solomon presume it lawful. Note, If those that are in reputation for religion in any thing set a bad example, they know not what a deal of mischief they may do by it, particularly to their own children. One bad act of a good man may be of more pernicious consequence to others than twenty of a wicked man. Probably Solomon, when he began to multiply wives, intended not to exceed his father's number. But the way of sin is down-hill; those that have got into it cannot easily stop themselves. Divine wisdom has appointed one woman for one man, did so at first; and those who do not think one enough will not think two or three enough. Unbridled lust will be unbounded, and the loosened hind will wander endlessly. But this was not all: (3.) They were strange women, Moabites, Ammonites, &c., of the nations which God had particularly forbidden them to intermarry with, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.2">v. 2</reference>. Some think it was in policy that he married these foreigners, by them to get intelligence of the state of those countries. I rather fear it was because the daughters of Israel were too grave and modest for him, and those foreigners pleased him with the looseness and wantonness of their dress, and air, and conversation. Or, perhaps, it was looked upon as a piece of state to have his seraglio, as his other treasures, replenished with that which was far-fetched; as if that were too great an honour for the best of his subjects which would really have been a disgrace to the meanest of them—to be his mistresses. And, (4.) To complete the mischief, <hi type="italic">Solomon clave unto these in love,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.2">v. 2</reference>. He not only kept them, but was extravagantly fond of them, set his heart upon them, spent his time among them, thought every thing well they said and did, and despised Pharaoh's daughter, his rightful wife, who had been dear to him, and all the ladies of Israel, in comparison of them. Solomon was master of a great deal of knowledge, but to what purpose, when he had no better a government of his appetites? <div eID="gen6740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6741" type="x-p"/> 2. He was drawn by them to the worship of strange gods, as Israel to Baal-peor by the daughters of Moab. This was the bad consequence of his multiplying wives. We have reason to think it impaired his health, and hastened upon him the decays of age; it exhausted his treasure, which, though vast indeed, would be found little enough to maintain the pride and vanity of all these women; perhaps it occasioned him, in his latter end, to neglect his business, by which he lost his supplies from abroad, and was forced, for the keeping up of his grandeur, to burden his subjects with those taxes which they complained of, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.4">ch. xii. 4</reference>. But none of these consequences were so bad as this: <hi type="italic">His wives turned away his heart after other gods,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.3-1Kgs.11.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. (1.) He grew cool and indifferent in his own religion and remiss in the service of the God of Israel: <hi type="italic">His heart was not perfect with the Lord his God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.4">v. 4</reference>), nor did he <hi type="italic">follow him fully</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.6">v. 6</reference>), like David. We cannot suppose that he quite cast off the worship of God, much less that he restrained or hindered it (the temple-service went on as usual); but he grew less frequent, and less serious, in <hi type="italic">his ascent to the house of the Lord</hi> and his attendance on his altar. He left his first love, lost his zeal for God, and did not persevere to the end as he had begun; therefore it is said <hi type="italic">he was not perfect,</hi> because he was not <hi type="italic">constant;</hi> and he followed not God fully, because he turned from following him, and did not continue to the end. His father David had many faults, but he never neglected the worship of God, nor grew remiss in that, as Solomon did (his wives using all their arts to divert him from it), and <hi type="italic">there</hi> began his apostasy. (2.) He tolerated and maintained his wives in their idolatry and made no scruple of joining with them in it. Pharaoh's daughter was proselyted (as is supposed) to the Jews' religion, but, when he began to grow careless in the worship of God himself, he used no means to convert his other wives to it; in complaisance to them, he built chapels for their gods (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.7-1Kgs.11.8">v. 7, 8</reference>), maintained their priests, and occasionally did himself attend their altars, making a jest of it, asking, "What harm is there in it? Are not all religions alike?" which (says bishop Patrick) has been the <hi type="italic">disease of some great wits.</hi> When he humoured one thus, the rest would take it ill if he did not, in like manner, gratify them, so that he did it for all his wives (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.8">v. 8</reference>), and at last came to such a degree of impiety that he set up a high place for <hi type="italic">Chemosh in the hill that is before Jerusalem,</hi> the <hi type="italic">mount of Olives,</hi> as if to confront the temple which he himself had built. These high places continued here, not utterly demolished, till Josiah's time, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.13">2 Kings xxiii. 13</reference>. This is the account here given of Solomon's apostasy. <div eID="gen6741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6742" type="x-p"/> II. Let us now pause awhile, and lament Solomon's fall; and we may justly stand and wonder at it. <hi type="italic">How has the gold become dim! How has the most fine gold changed! Be astonished, O heavens! at this, and be horribly afraid,</hi> as the prophet exclaims in a like case, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.12">Jer. ii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen6742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6743" type="x-p"/> 1. How strange, (1.) That Solomon, in his old age, should be ensnared with fleshly lusts, youthful lusts. As we must never presume upon the strength of our resolutions, so neither upon the weakness of our corruptions, so as to be secure and off our guard. (2.) That so wise a man as Solomon was, so famed for a quick understanding and sound judgment, should suffer himself to be made such a fool of by these foolish women. (3.) That one who had so often and so plainly warned others of the danger of the love of women should himself be so wretchedly bewitched with it; it is easier to see a mischief, and to show it to others, than to shun it ourselves. (4.) That so good a man, so zealous for the worship of God, who had been so conversant with divine things, and who prayed that excellent prayer at the dedication of the temple, should do these sinful things. Is this Solomon? Have all his wisdom and devotion come to this at last? Never was gallant ship so wrecked; never was crown so profaned. <div eID="gen6743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6744" type="x-p"/> 2. What shall we say to all this? Why God permitted it it is not for us to enquire; his way is in the sea and his path in the great waters; he knew how to bring glory to himself out of it. God foresaw it when he said concerning him that should build the temple, <hi type="italic">If he commit iniquity,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14">2 Sam. vii. 14</reference>. But it concerns us to enquire what good use we may make of it. (1.) Let him that thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. We see how weak we are of ourselves, without the grace of God; let us therefore live in a constant dependence on that grace. (2.) See the danger of a prosperous condition, and how hard it is to overcome the temptations of it. Solomon, like Jeshurun, waxed fat and then kicked. The food convenient, which Agur prayed for, is safer and better than the food abundant, which Solomon was even surfeited with. (3.) See what need those have to stand upon their guard who have made a great profession of religion, and shown themselves forward and zealous in devotion, because the devil will set upon them most violently, and, if they misbehave, the reproach is the greater. It is the evening that commends the day; let us therefore fear, lest, having run well, we seem to come short.
entries.ac03a2e5a6c903e3fd76e4dc0aed0c5302d83ff8: <div eID="gen6744" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Displeasure against Solomon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 983.)</title> <div sID="gen6745" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, which had appeared unto him twice, <hi type="super">10</hi> And had commanded him concerning this thing, that he should not go after other gods: but he kept not that which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded. <hi type="super">11</hi> Wherefore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Solomon, Forasmuch as this is done of thee, and thou hast not kept my covenant and my statutes, which I have commanded thee, I will surely rend the kingdom from thee, and will give it to thy servant. <hi type="super">12</hi> Notwithstanding in thy days I will not do it for David thy father's sake: <hi type="italic">but</hi> I will rend it out of the hand of thy son. <hi type="super">13</hi> Howbeit I will not rend away all the kingdom; <hi type="italic">but</hi> will give one tribe to thy son for David my servant's sake, and for Jerusalem's sake which I have chosen. <div eID="gen6745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6746" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. God's anger against Solomon for his sin. The thing he did <hi type="italic">displeased the Lord.</hi> Time was then the Lord <hi type="italic">loved Solomon</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.24">2 Sam. xii. 24</reference>) and delighted in him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.9">ch. x. 9</reference>), but now <hi type="italic">the Lord was angry with Solomon</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.9">v. 9</reference>), for there was in his sin, 1. The most base ingratitude that could be. He turned from the Lord <hi type="italic">who had appeared unto him twice,</hi> once before he began to build the temple (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.5">ch. iii. 5</reference>) and once after he had dedicated it, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.2">ch. ix. 2</reference>. God keeps account of the gracious visits he makes us, whether we do or no, knows how often he has appeared <hi type="italic">to</hi> us and <hi type="italic">for</hi> us, and will remember it against us if we <hi type="italic">turn from him.</hi> God's appearing to Solomon was such a sensible confirmation of his faith as should have for ever prevented his worshipping <hi type="italic">any other god;</hi> it was also such a distinguishing favour, and put such an honour upon him, as he ought never to have forgotten, especially considering what God said to him in both these appearances. 2. The most wilful disobedience. This was the very thing concerning which <hi type="italic">God had commanded him—that he should not go after other gods,</hi> yet he was not restrained by such an express admonition, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.10">v. 10</reference>. Those who have dominion over men are apt to forget God's dominion over them; and, while they demand obedience from their inferiors, to deny it to him who is the Supreme. <div eID="gen6746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6747" type="x-p"/> II. The message he sent him hereupon (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord said unto Solomon</hi> (it is likely by a prophet) that he must expect to smart for his apostasy. And here, 1. The sentence is just, that, since he had revolted from God, part of his kingdom should revolt from his family; he had given God's glory to the creature, and therefore God would give his crown to his servant: "<hi type="italic">I will rend the kingdom from thee,</hi> in thy posterity, and will <hi type="italic">give it to thy servant,</hi> who shall bear rule over much of that for which thou hast laboured." This was a great mortification to Solomon, who pleased himself no doubt with the prospect of the entail of his rich kingdom upon his heirs for ever. Sin brings ruin upon families, cuts off entails, alienates estates, and lays men's honour in the dust. 2. Yet the mitigations of it are very kind, for David's sake (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.12-1Kgs.11.13">v. 12, 13</reference>), that is, for the sake of the promise made to David. Thus all the favour God shows to man is for <hi type="italic">Christ's sake,</hi> and for the sake of the covenant made with him. The kingdom shall be rent from Solomon's house, but, (1.) Not immediately. Solomon shall not live to see it done, but it shall be rent <hi type="italic">out of the hand of his son,</hi> a son that was born to him by one of his strange wives, for his mother was an Ammonitess (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.31">1 Kings xiv. 31</reference>) and probably had been a promoter of idolatry. What comfort can a man take in leaving children and an estate behind him if he do not leave a blessing behind him? Yet, if judgments be coming, it is a favour to us if they come not in our days, as <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.19">2 Kings xx. 19</reference>. (2.) Not wholly. One tribe, that of Judah, the strongest and most numerous, shall remain to the house of David (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.13">v. 13</reference>), for Jerusalem's sake, which David built, and for the sake of the temple there, which Solomon built; these shall not go into other hands. Solomon did not quickly nor wholly turn away from God; therefore God did not quickly nor wholly take the kingdom from him. <div eID="gen6747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6748" type="x-p"/> Upon this message which God graciously sent to Solomon, to awaken his conscience and bring him to repentance, we have reason to hope that he humbled himself before God, confessed his sin, begged pardon, and returned to his duty, that he then published his repentance in the book of Ecclesiastes, where he bitterly laments his own folly and madness (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.25-Eccl.7.26">ch. vii. 25, 26</reference>), and warns others to take heed of the like evil courses, and to <hi type="italic">fear God</hi> and <hi type="italic">keep his commandments,</hi> in consideration of <hi type="italic">the judgment to come,</hi> which, it is likely, had made him tremble, as it did Felix. That penitential sermon was as true an indication of a heart broken for sin and turned from it as David's penitential psalms were, though of another nature. God's grace in his people works variously. Thus, though Solomon fell, <hi type="italic">he was not utterly cast down;</hi> what God had said to David concerning him was fulfilled: <hi type="italic">I will chasten him with the rod of men, but my mercy shall not depart from him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14-2Sam.7.15">2 Sam. vii. 14, 15</reference>. Though God may suffer those whom he loves to fall into sin, he will not suffer them to lie still in it. Solomon's defection, though it was much his reproach and a great blemish to his personal character, yet did not so far break in upon the character of his reign but that it was afterwards made the pattern of a good reign, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.17">2 Chron. xi. 17</reference>, where the kings are said to have done well, while <hi type="italic">they walked in the way of David and Solomon.</hi> But, though we have all this reason to hope he repented and found mercy, yet the Holy Ghost did not think fit expressly to record his recovery, but left it doubtful, for warning to others not to sin upon presumption of repenting, for it is but a peradventure whether <hi type="italic">God will give them repentance,</hi> or, if he do, whether he will give the evidence of it to themselves or others. Great sinners may recover themselves and have the benefit of their repentance, and yet be denied both the comfort and credit of it; the guilt may be taken away, and yet not the reproach.
entries.79c721725781358b61d20db7fb0baa7fc31aaba3: <div eID="gen6748" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Solomon's Adversaries. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 980.)</title> <div sID="gen6749" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> stirred up an adversary unto Solomon, Hadad the Edomite: he <hi type="italic">was</hi> of the king's seed in Edom. <hi type="super">15</hi> For it came to pass, when David was in Edom, and Joab the captain of the host was gone up to bury the slain, after he had smitten every male in Edom; <hi type="super">16</hi> (For six months did Joab remain there with all Israel, until he had cut off every male in Edom:) <hi type="super">17</hi> That Hadad fled, he and certain Edomites of his father's servants with him, to go into Egypt; Hadad <hi type="italic">being</hi> yet a little child. <hi type="super">18</hi> And they arose out of Midian, and came to Paran: and they took men with them out of Paran, and they came to Egypt, unto Pharaoh king of Egypt; which gave him a house, and appointed him victuals, and gave him land. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Hadad found great favour in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him to wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the sister of Tahpenes bare him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house: and Genubath was in Pharaoh's household among the sons of Pharaoh. <hi type="super">21</hi> And when Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers, and that Joab the captain of the host was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, Let me depart, that I may go to mine own country. <hi type="super">22</hi> Then Pharaoh said unto him, But what hast thou lacked with me, that, behold, thou seekest to go to thine own country? And he answered, Nothing: howbeit let me go in any wise. <hi type="super">23</hi> And God stirred him up <hi type="italic">another</hi> adversary, Rezon the son of Eliadah, which fled from his lord Hadadezer king of Zobah: <hi type="super">24</hi> And he gathered men unto him, and became captain over a band, when David slew them <hi type="italic">of Zobah:</hi> and they went to Damascus, and dwelt therein, and reigned in Damascus. <hi type="super">25</hi> And he was an adversary to Israel all the days of Solomon, beside the mischief that Hadad <hi type="italic">did:</hi> and he abhorred Israel, and reigned over Syria. <div eID="gen6749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6750" type="x-p"/> While Solomon kept closely to God and to his duty there was <hi type="italic">no adversary nor evil occurrent</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.4">ch. v. 4</reference>), nothing to create him any disturbance or uneasiness in the least; but here we have an account of two adversaries that appeared against him, inconsiderable, and that could not have done any thing worth taking notice of if Solomon had not first made God his enemy. What hurt could Hadad or Rezon have done to so great and powerful a king as Solomon was if he had not, by sin, made himself mean and weak? And then those little people menace and insult him. If God be on our side, we need not fear the greatest adversary; but, if he be against us, he can make us fear the least, and the very grasshopper shall be a burden. Observe, <div eID="gen6750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6751" type="x-p"/> I. Both these adversaries God stirred up, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.14">v. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.23">23</reference>. Though they themselves were moved by principles of ambition or revenge, God made use of them to serve his design of correcting Solomon. The principal judgment threatened was deferred, namely, the rending of the kingdom from him, but he himself was made to feel the smart of the rod, for his greater humiliation. Note, Whoever are, in any way, adversaries to us, we must take notice of the hand of God stirring them up to be so, as he bade Shimei curse David; we must look through the instruments of our trouble to the author of it and hear the Lord's controversy in it. <div eID="gen6751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6752" type="x-p"/> II. Both these adversaries had the origin of their enmity to Solomon and Israel laid in David's time, and in his conquests of their respective countries, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.15">v. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.24">24</reference>. Solomon had the benefit and advantage of his father's successes both in the enlargement of his dominion and the increase of his treasure, and would never have known any thing but the benefit of them if he had kept closely to God; but now he finds evils to balance the advantages, and that David had made himself enemies, who were thorns in his sides. Those that are too free in giving provocation ought to consider that perhaps it may be remembered in time to come and returned with interest to theirs after them; having so few friends in this world, it is our wisdom not to make ourselves more enemies than we needs must. <div eID="gen6752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6753" type="x-p"/> 1. Hadad, an Edomite, was an adversary to Solomon. We are not told what he did against him, nor which way he gave him disturbance, only, in general, that he was an adversary to him: but we are told, (1.) What induced him to bear Solomon a grudge. David had conquered Edom, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">2 Sam. viii. 14</reference>. Joab put all the males to the sword, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.15-1Kgs.11.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. A terrible execution he made, avenging on Edom their old enmity to Israel, yet perhaps with too great a severity. From this general slaughter, while Joab was burying the slain (for he left not any alive of their own people to bury them, and buried they must be, or they would be an annoyance to the country, <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.12">Ezek. xxxix. 12</reference>), Hadad, a branch of the royal family, then a little child, was taken and preserved by some of the king's servants, and conveyed to Egypt, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.17">v. 17</reference>. They halted by the way, in Midian first, and then in Paran, where they furnished themselves with men, not to fight for them or force their passage, but to attend them, that their young master might go into Egypt with an equipage agreeable to his quality. There he was kindly sheltered and entertained by Pharaoh, as a distressed prince, as well provided for, and so recommended himself that, in process of time, he married the queen's sister (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.19">v. 19</reference>), and by her had a child, which the queen herself conceived such a kindness for that she brought him up in Pharaoh's house, among the king's children. (2.) What enabled him to do Solomon a mischief. Upon the death of David and Joab, he returned to his own country, in which, it should seem, he settled and remained quiet while Solomon continued wise and watchful for the public good, but from which he had opportunity of making inroads upon Israel when Solomon, having sinned away his wisdom as Samson did his strength (and in the same way), grew careless of public affairs, was off his guard himself, and had forfeited the divine protection. What vexation Hadad gave to Solomon we are not here told, but only how loth Pharaoh was to part with him and how earnestly he solicited his stay (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">What hast thou lacked with me?</hi> "Nothing," says Hadad; "but let me go to my own country, my native air, my native soil." Peter Martyr has a pious reflection upon this: "Heaven is our home, and we ought to keep up a holy affection to that, and desire towards it, even when the world, the place of our banishment, smiles most upon us." Does it ask, What have you lacked, that you are so willing to be gone? We may answer, "Nothing that the world can do for us; but still let us go thither, where our hope, and honour, and treasure are." <div eID="gen6753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6754" type="x-p"/> 2. Rezon, a Syrian, was another adversary to Solomon. When David conquered the Syrians, he headed the remains, lived at large by spoil and rapine, till Solomon grew careless, and then he got possession of Damascus, reigned there (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.24">v. 24</reference>) and over the country about (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.25">v. 25</reference>), and he created troubles to Israel, probably in conjunction with Hadad, all the days of Solomon (namely, after his apostasy), or he was an enemy to Israel during all Solomon's reign, and upon all occasions vented his then impotent malice against them, but till Solomon's revolt, when his defence had departed from him, he could not do them any mischief. It is said of him that <hi type="italic">he abhorred Israel.</hi> Other princes loved and admired Israel and Solomon, and courted their friendship, but here was one that abhorred them. The greatest and best of princes and people, however much they may in general be respected, will yet perhaps be hated and abhorred by some.
entries.645442e7495b52c22dda8f4e56590dd712122c2b: <div eID="gen6754" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeroboam's Promotion Foretold. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 977.)</title> <div sID="gen6755" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> And Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephrathite of Zereda, Solomon's servant, whose mother's name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Zeruah, a widow woman, even he lifted up <hi type="italic">his</hi> hand against the king. <hi type="super">27</hi> And this <hi type="italic">was</hi> the cause that he lifted up <hi type="italic">his</hi> hand against the king: Solomon built Millo, <hi type="italic">and</hi> repaired the breaches of the city of David his father. <hi type="super">28</hi> And the man Jeroboam <hi type="italic">was</hi> a mighty man of valour: and Solomon seeing the young man that he was industrious, he made him ruler over all the charge of the house of Joseph. <hi type="super">29</hi> And it came to pass at that time when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, that the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him in the way; and he had clad himself with a new garment; and they two <hi type="italic">were</hi> alone in the field: <hi type="super">30</hi> And Ahijah caught the new garment that <hi type="italic">was</hi> on him, and rent it <hi type="italic">in</hi> twelve pieces: <hi type="super">31</hi> And he said to Jeroboam, Take thee ten pieces: for thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of Israel, Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee: <hi type="super">32</hi> (But he shall have one tribe for my servant David's sake, and for Jerusalem's sake, the city which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel:) <hi type="super">33</hi> Because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon, and have not walked in my ways, to do <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> right in mine eyes, and <hi type="italic">to keep</hi> my statutes and my judgments, as <hi type="italic">did</hi> David his father. <hi type="super">34</hi> Howbeit I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand: but I will make him prince all the days of his life for David my servant's sake, whom I chose, because he kept my commandments and my statutes: <hi type="super">35</hi> But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand, and will give it unto thee, <hi type="italic">even</hi> ten tribes. <hi type="super">36</hi> And unto his son will I give one tribe, that David my servant may have a light alway before me in Jerusalem, the city which I have chosen me to put my name there. <hi type="super">37</hi> And I will take thee, and thou shalt reign according to all that thy soul desireth, and shalt be king over Israel. <hi type="super">38</hi> And it shall be, if thou wilt hearken unto all that I command thee, and wilt walk in my ways, and do <hi type="italic">that is</hi> right in my sight, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did; that I will be with thee, and build thee a sure house, as I built for David, and will give Israel unto thee. <hi type="super">39</hi> And I will for this afflict the seed of David, but not for ever. <hi type="super">40</hi> Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam. And Jeroboam arose, and fled into Egypt, unto Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon. <div eID="gen6755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6756" type="x-p"/> We have here the first mention of that infamous name <hi type="italic">Jeroboam the son of Nebat, that made Israel to sin;</hi> he is here brought upon the stage as an adversary to Solomon, whom God had expressly told (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.11">v. 11</reference>) that he would give the greatest part of his kingdom to his servant, and Jeroboam was the man. We have here an account, <div eID="gen6756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6757" type="x-p"/> I. Of his extraction, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.26">v. 26</reference>. He was of the tribe of Ephraim, he next in honour to Judah. His mother was a widow, to whom Providence had made up the loss of a husband in a son that was active and ingenious, and (we may suppose) a great support and comfort to her. <div eID="gen6757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6758" type="x-p"/> II. Of his elevation. It was Solomon's wisdom, when he had work to do, to employ proper persons in it. He observed Jeroboam to be a very industrious young man, one that minded his business, took a pleasure in it, and did it with all his might, and therefore he gradually advanced him, till at length he made him receiver-general for the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, or perhaps put him into an office equivalent to that of lord-lieutenant of those two counties, for he was ruler of the burden, or tribute, that is, either of the taxes or of the militia of the house of Joseph. Note, Industry is the way to preferment. <hi type="italic">Seest thou a man diligent in his business,</hi> that will take care and pains, and go through with it? he shall <hi type="italic">stand before kings,</hi> and not always be on the level with mean men. Observe a difference between David, and both his predecessor and his successor: when Saul saw a <hi type="italic">valiant man he took him to himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.52">1 Sam. xiv. 52</reference>); when Solomon saw an <hi type="italic">industrious</hi> man he preferred him; but David's <hi type="italic">eyes were upon the faithful in the land,</hi> that they might <hi type="italic">dwell with him:</hi> if he saw a godly man, he preferred him, for he was a man after God's own heart, whose <hi type="italic">countenance beholds the upright.</hi> <div eID="gen6758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6759" type="x-p"/> III. Of his designation to the government of the ten tribes after the death of Solomon. Some think he was himself plotting against Solomon, and contriving to rise to the throne, that he was turbulent and aspiring. The Jews say that when he was employed by Solomon in building Millo he took opportunities of reflecting upon Solomon as oppressive to his people, and suggesting that which would alienate them from his government. It is not indeed probable that he should say much to that purport, for Solomon would have got notice of it, and it would have hindered his preferment; but it is plainly intimated that he had it in his thoughts, for the prophet tells him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.37">v. 37</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou shalt reign according to all that thy soul desireth.</hi> But this was the <hi type="italic">cause,</hi> or rather this was the <hi type="italic">story,</hi> of the lifting up of his hand against the king: Solomon made him ruler over the tribes of Joseph, and, as he was going to take possession of his government, he was told by a prophet in God's name that he should be king, which emboldened him to aim high, and in some instances to oppose the king and give him vexation. 1. The prophet by whom this message was sent was <hi type="italic">Ahijah of Shiloh;</hi> we shall read of him again, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.2">ch. xiv. 2</reference>. It seems, Shiloh was not so perfectly forsaken and forgotten of God but that, in remembrance of the former days, it was blessed with a prophet. He delivered his message to Jeroboam in the way, his servants being probably ordered to retire, as in a like case (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.27">1 Sam. ix. 27</reference>), when Samuel delivered his message to Saul. God's word was not the less sacred and sure for being delivered to him thus obscurely, under a hedge it may be. 2. The sign by which it was represented to him was the rending of a garment into twelve pieces, and giving him ten, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.30-1Kgs.11.31">v. 30, 31</reference>. It is not certain whether the garment was Jeroboam's, as is commonly taken for granted, or Ahijah's, which is more probable: <hi type="italic">He</hi> (that is, the prophet) <hi type="italic">had clad himself with a new garment,</hi> on purpose that he might with it give him a sign. The rending of the kingdom from Saul was signified by the rending of Samuel's mantle, not Saul's, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.27-1Sam.15.28">1 Sam. xv. 27, 28</reference>. And it was more significant to give Jeroboam ten pieces of that which was not his own before than of that which was. The prophets, both true and false, used such signs, even in the New Testament, as Agabus, <reference osisRef="Acts.21.10-Acts.21.11">Acts xxi. 10, 11</reference>. 3. The message itself, which is very particular, (1.) He assures him that he shall be king over ten of the twelve tribes of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.31">v. 31</reference>. The meanness of his extraction and employment shall be no hindrance to his advancement, when the God of Israel says (by whom kings reign), <hi type="italic">I will give ten tribes unto thee.</hi> (2.) He tells him the reason; not for his good character or deserts, but for the chastising of Solomon's apostasy: "Because he, and his family, and many of his people with him, <hi type="italic">have forsaken me, and worshipped other gods,</hi>" <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.33">v. 33</reference>. It was because they had done ill, not because he was likely to do much better. Thus Israel must know that it is not <hi type="italic">for their righteousness</hi> that they are made masters of Canaan, but for the wickedness of the Canaanites, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.4">Deut. ix. 4</reference>. Jeroboam did not deserve so good a post, but Israel deserved so bad a prince. In telling him that the reason why he rent the kingdom from the house of Solomon was because they had forsaken God, he warns him to take heed of sinning away his preferment in like manner. (3.) He limits his expectations to the ten tribes only, and to them in reversion after the death of Solomon, lest he should aim at the whole and give immediate disturbance to Solomon's government. He is here told, [1.] That two tribes (called here <hi type="italic">one tribe,</hi> because little Benjamin was in a manner lost in the thousands of Judah) should remain sure to the house of David, and he must never make any attempt upon them: <hi type="italic">He shall have one tribe</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.32">v. 32</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.36">v. 36</reference>), <hi type="italic">That David may have a lamp,</hi> that is, a shining name and memory (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.17">Ps. cxxxii. 17</reference>), and his family, as a royal family, may not be extinct. He must not think that David was rejected, as Saul was. No, God would not take his loving-kindness from him, as he did from Saul. The house of David must be supported and kept in reputation, for all this, because out of it the Messiah must arise. <hi type="italic">Destroy it not,</hi> for that <hi type="italic">blessing is in it.</hi> [2.] That Solomon must keep possession during his life, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.34-1Kgs.11.35">v. 34, 35</reference>. Jeroboam therefore must not offer to dethrone him, but wait with patience till his day shall come to fall. Solomon shall be <hi type="italic">prince, all the days of his life,</hi> not for his own sake (he had forfeited his crown to the justice of God), but for <hi type="italic">David my servant's sake, because he kept my commandments.</hi> Children that do not tread in their parents' steps yet often fare the better in this world for their good parents' piety. (4.) He gives him to understand that he will be upon his good behaviour. The grant of the crown must run <hi type="italic">quamdiu se bene gesserit—during good behaviour.</hi> "If thou wilt <hi type="italic">do what is right in my sight, I will build thee a sure house,</hi> and not otherwise" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.38">v. 38</reference>), intimating that, if he forsook God, even his advancement to the throne would in time lay his family in the dust; whereas the seed of David, though afflicted, should not be afflicted for ever (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.39">v. 39</reference>), but should flourish again, as it did in many of the illustrious kings of Judah, who reigned in glory when Jeroboam's family was extirpated. <div eID="gen6759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6760" type="x-p"/> IV. Jeroboam's flight into Egypt, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.40">v. 40</reference>. In some way or other Solomon came to know of all this, probably from Jeroboam's own talk of it; he could not conceal it as Saul did, nor keep his own counsel; if he had, he might have staid in his country, and been preparing there for his future advancement; but letting it be known, 1. Solomon foolishly sought to kill his successor. Had not he taught others that, whatever devices are in men's hearts, <hi type="italic">the counsel of the Lord shall stand?</hi> And yet does he himself think to defeat that counsel? 2. Jeroboam prudently withdrew into Egypt. Though God's promise would have secured him any where, yet he would use means for his own preservation, and was content to live in exile and obscurity for a while, being sure of a kingdom at last. And shall not we be so, who have a better kingdom in reserve?
entries.c4a41ba08dd6e2d3dac8300ecbdf3d7746994b62: <div eID="gen6760" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Death of Solomon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 975.)</title> <div sID="gen6761" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">41</hi> And the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, <hi type="italic">are</hi> they not written in the book of the acts of Solomon? <hi type="super">42</hi> And the time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel <hi type="italic">was</hi> forty years. <hi type="super">43</hi> And Solomon slept with his fathers, and was buried in the city of David his father: and Rehoboam his son reigned in his stead. <div eID="gen6761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6762" type="x-p"/> We have here the conclusion of Solomon's story, and in it, 1. Reference is had to another history then extant, but (not being divinely inspired) since lost, <hi type="italic">the Book of the Acts of Solomon,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.41">v. 41</reference>. Probably this book was written by a chronologer or historiographer, whom Solomon employed to write his annals, out of which the sacred writer extracted what God saw fit to transmit to the church. 2. A summary of the years of his reign (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.42">v. 42</reference>): <hi type="italic">He reigned in Jerusalem</hi> (not, as his father, part of his time in Hebron and part in Jerusalem), <hi type="italic">over all Israel</hi> (not as his son, and his father in the beginning of his time, over Judah only), <hi type="italic">forty years.</hi> His reign was as long as his father's, but not his life. Sin shortened his days. 3. His death and burial, and his successor, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.43">v. 43</reference>. (1.) He followed his fathers to the grave, slept with them, and was buried in David's burying-place, with honour no doubt. (2.) His son followed him in the throne. Thus the graves are filling with the generations that go off, and houses are filling with those that are growing up. As the grave cries, "Give, give," so land is never lost for want of an heir.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.11"/> <div eID="gen6762" type="x-p"/>

entries.df46ae1b6ff6ec96812ca42360abecbeefde5fcf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3203"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <div sID="gen4478" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.1-1Kgs.11.8">1Ki 11:1-8</reference>. Solomon's Wives and Concubines in His Old Age.<div eID="gen4478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4479" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3203"/><hi type="bold">1-2. But King Solomon loved many strange women--</hi>Solomon's extraordinary gift of wisdom was not sufficient to preserve him from falling into grievous and fatal errors. A fairer promise of true greatness, a more beautiful picture of juvenile piety, never was seen than that which he exhibited at the commencement of his reign. No sadder, more humiliating, or awful spectacle can be imagined than the besotted apostasy of his old age; and to him may be applied the words of Paul (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.3">Ga 3:3</reference>), of John (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.17">Re 3:17</reference>), and of Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.21">Is 14:21</reference>). A love of the world, a ceaseless round of pleasure, had insensibly corrupted his heart, and produced, for a while at least, a state of mental darkness. The grace of God deserted him; and the son of the pious David--the religiously trained child of Bath-sheba (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.1-Prov.31.3">Pr 31:1-3</reference>), and pupil of Nathan, instead of showing the stability of sound principle and mature experience became at last an old and foolish king (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.13">Ec 4:13</reference>). His fall is traced to his "love of many strange women." Polygamy was tolerated among the ancient Hebrews; and, although in most countries of the East, the generality of men, from convenience and economy, confine themselves to one woman, yet a number of wives is reckoned as an indication of wealth and importance, just as a numerous stud of horses and a grand equipage are among us. The sovereign, of course, wishes to have a more numerous harem than any of his subjects; and the female establishments of many Oriental princes have, both in ancient and modern times, equalled or exceeded that of Solomon's. It is probable, therefore, that, in conformity with Oriental notions, he resorted to it as a piece of state magnificence. But in him it was unpardonable, as it was a direct and outrageous violation of the divine law (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.17">De 17:17</reference>), and the very result which that statute was ordained to prevent was realized in him. His marriage with the daughter of Pharaoh is not censured either here or elsewhere (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.1">1Ki 3:1</reference>). It was only his love for many strange women; for women, though in the East considered inferiors, exert often a silent but powerful seductive influence over their husbands in the harem, as elsewhere, and so it was exemplified in Solomon. <div eID="gen4479" type="x-p"/>
entries.81498b77590dfaf90a2793e92588340913f2c00f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3204"/><div sID="gen4480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3204"/><hi type="bold">3. he had seven hundred wives, princesses--</hi>They were, probably, according to an existing custom, the daughters of tributary chiefs, given as hostages for good conduct of their fathers.<div eID="gen4480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4481" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">concubines--</hi>were legitimate, but lower or secondary wives. These the chief or first wife regards without the smallest jealousy or regret, as they look up to her with feelings of respectful submission. Solomon's wives became numerous, not all at once, but gradually. Even at an early period his taste for Oriental show seems to have led to the establishment of a considerable harem (<reference osisRef="Song.6.8">So 6:8</reference>). <div eID="gen4481" type="x-p"/>
entries.daca739c546d5cd5b3676261b7dab3342f897cfa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3205"/><div sID="gen4482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3205"/><hi type="bold">4. when Solomon was old--</hi>He could not have been more than fifty.<div eID="gen4482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his wives turned away his heart after other gods--</hi>Some, considering the lapse of Solomon into idolatry as a thing incredible, regard him as merely humoring his wives in the practice of their superstition; and, in countenancing their respective rites by his presence, as giving only an outward homage--a sensible worship, in which neither his understanding nor his heart was engaged. The apology only makes matters worse, as it implies an adding of hypocrisy and contempt of God to an open breach of His law. There seems no possibility of explaining the language of the sacred historian, but as intimating that Solomon became an actual and open idolater, worshipping images of wood or stone in sight of the very temple which, in early life, he had erected to the true God. Hence that part of Olivet was called the high place of Tophet (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.30-Jer.7.34">Jr 7:30-34</reference>), and the hill is still known as the Mount of Offense, of the Mount of Corruption (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.13">2Ki 23:13</reference>). <div eID="gen4483" type="x-p"/>
entries.e64a7ed3978bd3efc9a60d8f82523c9636f28564: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3206"/><div sID="gen4484" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3206"/><hi type="bold">5-7. Ashtoreth--</hi>Astarte,<div eID="gen4484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4485" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Milcom--</hi>Molech,<div eID="gen4485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4486" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and Chemosh--</hi>He built altars for these three; but, although he is described (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.8">1Ki 11:8</reference>) as doing the same for "all his strange wives," there is no evidence that they had idols distinct from these; and there is no trace whatever of Egyptian idolatry. <div eID="gen4486" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c1f78e8f4b6265f452d8347b1e852cc394c872a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3207"/><div sID="gen4487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3207"/><hi type="bold">8. burnt incense and sacrificed unto their gods--</hi>The first was considered a higher act of homage, and is often used as synonymous with worship (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.17">2Ki 22:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">23:5</reference>).<div eID="gen4487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4488" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.9-1Kgs.11.13">1Ki 11:9-13</reference>. God Threatens Him. <div eID="gen4488" type="x-p"/>
entries.f423b69333210311f325f1c6a320ec93354f34f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3208"/><div sID="gen4489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3208"/><hi type="bold">9-12. the Lord was angry with Solomon--</hi>The divine appearance, first at Gibeon [1Ki 3:5], and then at Jerusalem [1Ki 9:2], after the dedication of the temple, with the warnings given him on both occasions [1Ki 3:11-14; 9:3-9], had left Solomon inexcusable; and it was proper and necessary that on one who had been so signally favored with the gifts of Heaven, but who had grossly abused them, a terrible judgment should fall. The divine sentence was announced to him probably by Ahijah; but there was mercy mingled with judgment, in the circumstance, that it should not be inflicted on Solomon personally--and that a remnant of the kingdom should be spared--"for David's sake, and for Jerusalem's sake, which had been chosen" to put God's name there; not from a partial bias in favor of either, but that the divine promise might stand (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.12-2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:12-16</reference>). <div eID="gen4489" type="x-p"/>
entries.936adeb0194441c405f4ae07ee3e27becd28931f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3209"/><div sID="gen4490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3209"/><hi type="bold">13. I will give one tribe to thy son--</hi>There were left to Rehoboam the tribes of Judah, Benjamin, and Levi (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.12">2Ch 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.13">13</reference>); and multitudes of Israelites, who, after the schism of the kingdom, established their residence within the territory of Judah to enjoy the privileges of the true religion (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.17">1Ki 12:17</reference>). These are all reckoned as one tribe.<div eID="gen4490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4491" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.14-1Kgs.11.40">1Ki 11:14-40</reference>. Solomon's Adversaries. <div eID="gen4491" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2ddb58310b354f56243c59815dad477df1d9043: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3210"/><div sID="gen4492" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3210"/><hi type="bold">14-25. the Lord stirred up an adversary--</hi>that is, permitted him, through the impulse of his own ambition, or revenge, to attack Israel. During the war of extermination, which Joab carried on in Edom (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.13">2Sa 8:13</reference>), this Hadad, of the royal family, a mere boy when rescued from the sword of the ruthless conqueror, was carried into Egypt, hospitably entertained, and became allied with the house of the Egyptian king. In after years, the thought of his native land and his lost kingdom taking possession of his mind, he, on learning the death of David and Joab, renounced the ease, possessions, and glory of his Egyptian residence, to return to Edom and attempt the recovery of his ancestral throne. The movements of this prince seem to have given much annoyance to the Hebrew government; but as he was defeated by the numerous and strong garrisons planted throughout the Edomite territory, Hadad seems to have offered his services to Rezon, another of Solomon's adversaries (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.23-1Kgs.11.25">1Ki 11:23-25</reference>). This man, who had been general of Hadadezer and, on the defeat of that great king, had successfully withdrawn a large force, went into the wilderness, led a predatory life, like Jephthah, David, and others, on the borders of the Syrian and Arabian deserts. Then, having acquired great power, he at length became king in Damascus, threw off the yoke, and was "the adversary of Israel all the days of Solomon." He was succeeded by Hadad, whose successors took the official title of Ben-hadad from him, the illustrious founder of the powerful kingdom of Damascene-Syria. These hostile neighbors, who had been long kept in check by the traditional fame of David's victories, took courage; and breaking out towards the latter end of Solomon's reign, they must have not only disturbed his kingdom by their inroads, but greatly crippled his revenue by stopping his lucrative traffic with Tadmor and the Euphrates. <div eID="gen4492" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ed4add1482f93ff2a727cc051cb3d57514f2bd6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3211"/><div sID="gen4493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3211"/><hi type="bold">26-40. Jeroboam--</hi>This was an internal enemy of a still more formidable character. He was a young man of talent and energy, who, having been appointed by Solomon superintendent of the engineering works projected around Jerusalem, had risen into public notice, and on being informed by a very significant act of the prophet Ahijah of the royal destiny which, by divine appointment, awaited him, his mind took a new turn. <div eID="gen4493" type="x-p"/>

entries.0c9457760a137fca15bd74fdf42b6907d5f25bc3: <div eID="gen11848" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen11849" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11850" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11850" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11849" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11851" type="x-p"/> Solomon's attachment to strange women, and consequent idolatry, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.1">1Kgs 11:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.2">1Kgs 11:2</reference>. Number of his wives and concubines, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.3">1Kgs 11:3</reference>. In his old age they turn away his heart from God, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.4">1Kgs 11:4</reference>. He builds temples to idols, burns incense and sacrifices to them, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.5-1Kgs.11.8">1Kgs 11:5-8</reference>. The Lord is angry with him, and threatens to deprive him of the kingdom, but will leave one tribe for David's sake, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.9-1Kgs.11.13">1Kgs 11:9-13</reference>. The Lord stirs up Hadad, the Edomite, to be his enemy; the history of this man, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.14-1Kgs.11.22">1Kgs 11:14-22</reference>. He stirs another adversary against him, Rezon the son of Eliadah. He and Hadad plague Israel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.23-1Kgs.11.25">1Kgs 11:23-25</reference>. Jeroboam also becomes his enemy, and the reason why, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.26-1Kgs.11.28">1Kgs 11:26-28</reference>. Ahijah the prophet meets Jeroboam, and promises, in the name of the Lord, that God will rend Israel from the family of Solomon, and give him ten tribes, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.29-1Kgs.11.39">1Kgs 11:29-39</reference>. Solomon, hearing of this, seeks to put Jeroboam to death, who escapes to Egypt, where he continues till the death of Solomon, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.40">1Kgs 11:40</reference>. Solomon dies, after having reigned over Israel forty years; and his son Rehoboam reigns in his stead, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.41-1Kgs.11.43">1Kgs 11:41-43</reference>. <div eID="gen11851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11852" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen11852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11853" type="x-p"/> Many strange women - That is, idolaters; together with the daughter of Pharaoh: she was also one of those strange women and an idolater. But many think she became a proselyte to the Jewish religion; of this there is no evidence.
entries.ed7df1b056ff9380ca5999047773c704be7d8d93: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen11853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11854" type="x-p"/> He had seven hundred wives, princesses - How he could get so many of the blood royal from the different surrounding nations, is astonishing; but probably the daughters of noblemen, generals, etc., may be included. <div eID="gen11854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11855" type="x-p"/> And three hundred concubines - These were wives of the second rank, who were taken according to the usages of those times; but their offspring could not inherit. Sarah was to Abraham what these seven hundred princesses were to Solomon; and the three hundred concubines stood in the same relation to the Israelitish king as Hagar and Keturah did to the patriarch. <div eID="gen11855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11856" type="x-p"/> Here then are one thousand wives to form this great bad man's harem! Was it possible that such a person could have any piety to God, who was absorbed by such a number of women? We scarcely allow a man to have the fear of God who has a second wife or mistress; in what state then must the man be who has one thousand of them? We may endeavor to excuse all this by saying, "It was a custom in the East to have a multitude of women, and that there were many of those whom Solomon probably never saw," etc., etc. But was there any of them whom he might not have seen? Was it for reasons of state, or merely court splendor, that he had so many? How then is it said that he loved many strange women? - that he clave to them in love? And did he not give them the utmost proofs of his attachment when he not only tolerated their iniquitous worship in the land, but built temples to their idols, and more, burnt incense to them himself? As we should not condemn what God justifies, so we should not justify what God condemns. He went after Ashtaroth, the impure Venus of the Sidonians; after Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites; after Chemosh, the abomination of the Moabites; and after the murderous Molech, the abomination of the children of Ammon. He seems to have gone as far in iniquity as it was possible.
entries.0fb12f81f363d1c002a503b8617c6a9daa910304: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen11856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11857" type="x-p"/> The hill that is before Jerusalem - This was the Mount of Olives.
entries.2a7d3ea237647aac3f7e36af3a8c76a2dfd95021: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen11857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11858" type="x-p"/> The Lord was angry with Solomon - Had not this man's delinquency been strongly marked by the Divine disapprobation, it would have had a fatal effect on the morals of mankind. Vice is vice, no matter who commits it. And God is as much displeased with sin in Solomon as he can be with it in the most profligate, uneducated wretch. And although God sees the same sin in precisely the same degree of moral turpitude as to the act itself, yet there may be circumstances which greatly aggravate the offense, and subject the offender to greater punishment. Solomon was wise; he knew better; his understanding showed him the vanity as well as the wickedness of idolatry. God had appeared unto him twice, and thus given him the most direct proof of his being and of his providence. The promises of God had been fulfilled to him in the most remarkable manner, and in such a way as to prove that they came by a Divine counsel, and not by any kind of casualty. All these were aggravations of Solomon's crimes, as to their demerit; for the same crime has, in every case, the same degree of moral turpitude in the sight of God; but circumstances may so aggravate, as to require the offender to be more grievously punished; so the punishment may be legally increased where the crime is the same. Solomon deserved more punishment for his worship of Ashtaroth than any of the Sidonians did, though they performed precisely the same acts. The Sidonians had never known the true God; Solomon had been fully acquainted with him.
entries.23449a3b8c5d3af735527cbf8229e37da6b985fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen11858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11859" type="x-p"/> Forasmuch as this is done of thee - Was not this another warning from the Lord? And might not Solomon have yet recovered himself? Was there not mercy in this message which he might have sought and found?
entries.3b369b5347e905d1a05ee31d37961a6336e4420d: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen11859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11860" type="x-p"/> Will give one tribe - for David my servant's sake - The line of the Messiah must be preserved. The prevailing lion must come out of the tribe of Judah: not only the tribe must be preserved, but the regal line and the regal right. All this must be done for the true David's sake: and this was undoubtedly what God had in view by thus miraculously preserving the tribe of Judah and the royal line, in the midst of so general a defection. <div eID="gen11860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11861" type="x-p"/> And for Jerusalem's sake - As David was a type of the Messiah, so was Jerusalem a type of the true Church: therefore the Old Jerusalem must be preserved in the hands of the tribe of Judah, till the true David should establish the New Jerusalem in the same land, and in the same city. And what a series of providences did it require to do all these things!
entries.4183a42e205e9ea6f08a9f71299ad89414163ba1: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen11861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11862" type="x-p"/> The Lord stirred up an adversary - A satan, שטן. When he sent to Hiram to assist him in building the temple of the Lord, he could say, There was no satan, see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.4">1Kgs 5:4</reference>; and all his kingdom was in peace and security, - every man dwelt under his vine, and under his fig tree, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.25">1Kgs 4:25</reference> : but now that he had turned away from God, three satans rise up against him at once, Hadad, Rezon, and Jeroboam.
entries.179e4c9e90ad03a0fa47917fe88b43cc30b7059b: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen11862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11863" type="x-p"/> Was gone up to bury the slain - The slain Edomites; for Joab had in the course of six months exterminated all the males, except Hadad and his servants, who escaped to Egypt. Instead of bury the slain, the Targum has to take the spoils of the slain.
entries.391c6f8541d95a2c90d46b8f8a58522bb9d17067: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen11863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11864" type="x-p"/> Hadad being yet a little child - נער קטן naar katan, a little boy; one who was apprehensive of his danger, and could, with his father's servants, make his escape: not an infant.
entries.bead014fb58adf3477e5acbb66c33823ecb7fd91: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen11864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11865" type="x-p"/> These arose out of Midian - They at first retired to Midian, which lay to the southwest of the Dead Sea. Not supposing themselves in safety there, they went afterwards to Paran in the south of Idumea, and getting a number of persons to join them in Paran, they went straight to Egypt, where we find Hadad became a favourite with Pharaoh, who gave him his sister-in-law to wife; and incorporated him and his family with his own.
entries.4e9d5182bc97467b514b09acccdb64eaca42390a: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen11865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11866" type="x-p"/> Let me go in any wise - It does not appear that he avowed his real intention to Pharaoh; for at this time there must have been peace between Israel and Egypt, Solomon having married the daughter of Pharaoh.
entries.7cbdb402d300c5a528b5810467af520a8ed44c1e: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen11866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11867" type="x-p"/> Rezon the son of Eliadah - Thus God fulfilled his threatening by the prophet Nathan: If he commit iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men, and with the stripes of the children of men; <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14">2Sam 7:14</reference>.
entries.f81dc155bd899ef29fd6c924e6281fefbba274aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen11867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11868" type="x-p"/> And reigned in Damascus - Rezon was one of the captains of Hadadezer, whom David defeated. It seems that at this time Rezon escaped with his men; and; having lived, as is supposed, some time by plunder, he seized on Damascus, and reigned there till David took Damascus, when he subdued Syria, and drove out Rezon. But after Solomon's defection from God, Rezon, finding that God had departed from Israel, recovered Damascus; and joining with Hadad, harassed Solomon during the remaining part of his reign. But some think that Hadad and Rezon were the same person.
entries.4a521e9752dd38227901dd9a87562934b45eb046: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen11868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11869" type="x-p"/> Jeroboam the son of Nebat - From the context we learn that Jeroboam while a young man was employed by Solomon to superintend the improvements and buildings at Millo, and had so distinguished himself there by his industry and good conduct as to attract general notice, and to induce Solomon to set him over all the laborers employed in that work, belonging to the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, called here the house of Joseph. At first it appears that Solomon employed none of the Israelites in any drudgery; but it is likely that, as he grew profane, he grew tyrannical and oppressive: and at the works of Millo he changed his conduct; and there, in all probability, were the seeds of disaffection sown. And Jeroboam, being a clever and enterprising man, knew well how to avail himself of the general discontent.
entries.c5786dc709ed1281d4fc29b5387b1dcc2ee136ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen11869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11870" type="x-p"/> When Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem - On what errand he was going out of Jerusalem, we know not. <div eID="gen11870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11871" type="x-p"/> Ahijah the Shilonite - He was one of those who wrote the history of the reign of Solomon, as we find from <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.29">2Chr 9:29</reference>, and it is supposed that it was by him God spake twice to Solomon; and particularly delivered the message which we find in this chapter, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.11-1Kgs.11.13">1Kgs 11:11-13</reference>.
entries.ea27d41bab1124f1a0f0541abd08999a9a2373ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen11871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11872" type="x-p"/> Take thee ten pieces - The garment was the symbol of the kingdom of Israel; the twelve pieces the symbol of the twelve tribes; the ten pieces given to Jeroboam, of the ten tribes which should be given to him, and afterwards form the kingdom of Israel, ruling in Samaria, to distinguish it from the kingdom of Judah, ruling in Jerusalem.
entries.06746cbb9bbe8836bc7c58cd095fa1c95fbcd5d0: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen11872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11873" type="x-p"/> That David my servant may have a light alway - That his posterity may never fail, and the regal line never become extinct. This, as we have already seen, was in reference to the Messiah. He was not only David's light, but he was a light to enlighten the Gentiles.
entries.4a25d8be7cf7394e73a0e69e157731784a78fc2f: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen11873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11874" type="x-p"/> According to all that thy soul desireth - It appears from this that Jeroboam had affected the kingdom, and was seeking for an opportunity to seize on the government. God now tells him, by his prophet, what he shall have, and what he shall not have, in order to prevent him from attempting to seize on the whole kingdom, to the prejudice of the spiritual seed of David.
entries.cfde4c8ea7b4ecd2b1e360c1faf639fd76d32cc2: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen11874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11875" type="x-p"/> And build thee a sure house - He would have continued his posterity on the throne of Israel, had he not by his wickedness forfeited the promises of God, and thrown himself out of the protection of the Most High.
entries.654d7e6c0430a7ce42b5744271238acfd079d9ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen11875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11876" type="x-p"/> But not for ever - They shall be in affliction and distress till the Messiah come, who shall sit on the throne of David to order it and establish it in judgment and justice for ever. Jarchi says, on this verse, "When the Messiah comes, the kingdom shall be restored to the house of David.
entries.329b7bcd1c5df0eccbd3253c2b509d4540971432: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen11876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11877" type="x-p"/> Sought - to kill Jeroboam - He thought by this means to prevent the punishment due to his crimes. <div eID="gen11877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11878" type="x-p"/> Unto Shishak king of Egypt - This is the first time we meet with the proper name of an Egyptian king, Pharaoh being the common name for all the sovereigns of that country. Some suppose that this Shishak was the Sesostris so renowned for his wars and his conquests. But it is likely that this king lived long before Solomon's time.
entries.09f8cb0914a2504ce35445a78eca9888ea91e19f: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen11878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11879" type="x-p"/> The book of the acts of Solomon? - These acts were written by Nathan the prophet, Ahijah the Shilonite, and Iddo the seer; as we learn from <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.29">2Chr 9:29</reference>. Probably from these were the Books of Kings and Chronicles composed; but the original documents are long since lost.
entries.3dadb30a6f2dc09768704db486798995180b5292: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen11879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11880" type="x-p"/> Solomon reigned - forty years - Josephus says fourscore years, which is sufficiently absurd. Calmet supposes him to have been eighteen years old when he came to the throne, and that he died A.M. 3029, aged fifty-eight years; and, when we consider the excess in which he lived, and the criminal passions which he must have indulged among his thousand wives, and their idolatrous and impure worship, this life was as long as could be reasonably expected.
entries.f0af31fcece6c93f34c9cd7b052317467e20173f: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen11880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11881" type="x-p"/> Solomon slept with his fathers - He died in almost the flower of his age, and, it appears unregretted. His government was no blessing to Israel; and laid, by its exactions and oppressions, the foundation of that schism which was so fatal to the unhappy people of Israel and Judah, and was the most powerful procuring cause of the miseries which have fallen upon the Jewish people from that time until now. <div eID="gen11881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11882" type="x-p"/> I. It may now be necessary to give a more distinct outline of the character of this king. <div eID="gen11882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11883" type="x-p"/> 1. In his infancy and youth he had the high honor of being peculiarly loved by the Lord; and he had a name given him by the express authority of God himself, which to himself and others must ever call to remembrance this peculiar favor of the Most High. <div eID="gen11883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11884" type="x-p"/> There is little doubt that he was a most amiable youth, and his whole conduct appeared to justify the high expectations that were formed of him. <div eID="gen11884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11885" type="x-p"/> 2. He ascended the Israelitish throne at a time the most favorable for the cultivation of those arts so necessary to the comfort and improvement of life. Among all the surrounding nations Israel had not one open enemy; there was neither adversary, nor evil occurrent, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.4">1Kgs 5:4</reference>. He had rest on every side, and from the universal and profound peace which he enjoyed, the very important name Jedidiah, "beloved of the Lord" which was given him by Divine authority was changed to that of Solomon, the Peaceable, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.24">2Sam 12:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.25">2Sam 12:25</reference>, which at once indicated the state of the country, and the character of his own mild, pacific mind. <div eID="gen11885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11886" type="x-p"/> 3. To the dying charge of his pious father relative to the building a temple for the Lord, he paid the most punctual attention. He was fond of architecture, as we may learn from the account that is given of his numerous buildings and improvements; and yet it does not appear that he at all excelled in architectural knowledge. Hiram, the amiable king of Tyre, and his excellent workmen, were the grand directors and executors of the whole. By his public buildings he doubtless rendered Jerusalem highly respectable; but his passion for such works was not on the whole an advantage to his subjects, as it obliged him to have recourse to a burdensome system of taxation, which at first oppressed and exasperated his people, and ultimately led to the fatal separation of Israel and Judah. <div eID="gen11886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11887" type="x-p"/> 4. That he improved the trade and commerce of his country is sufficiently evident: by his public buildings vast multitudes were employed; and knowledge in the most beneficial arts must have been greatly increased, and the spirit of industry highly cultivated. <div eID="gen11887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11888" type="x-p"/> Commerce does not appear to have been much regarded, if even known, in Israel, previously to the days of Solomon. The most celebrated maritime power then in the world was that of the Tyrians. With great address and prudence he availed himself of their experience and commercial knowledge, sent his ships in company with theirs to make long and dangerous but lucrative voyages, and, by getting their sailors aboard of his own vessels, gained possession of their nautical skill, and also a knowledge of those safe ports in which they harboured, and of the rich countries with which they traded. His friendly alliance with the king of Tyre was a source of advantage to Israel, and might have been much more so had it been prudently managed. But after the time of Solomon we find it scarcely mentioned, and therefore it does not appear that the Jews continued to follow a track which had been so successfully opened to them; their endless contentions, and the ruinous wars of the two kingdoms, paralyzed all their commercial exertions: till at length all the maritime skill which they had acquired from the expert and industrious Tyrians, dwindled down to the puny art of managing a few boats on the internal lakes of their own country. Had it not been for the destructive feuds that reigned between the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah, that country might have become one of the best and richest maritime powers of either Asia or Europe.
